blocks.content: You type a message, or click a link, and hit send. A fraction of a second later something happens on a screen that might be sitting on the other side of the planet. In between those two moments, an enormous amount of coordinated work took place, and almost none of it is visible to you.

Earlier topics in this module looked at the layers a network stack is built from and the addresses that identify every device on it. This topic puts those pieces in motion. It traces one single journey, from the instant you hit send to the instant the message lands, so that everything you have learned so far has an actual story to live inside.

blocks.content: 1. A Click, and a Fraction of a Second Later
blocks.text: 1. A Click, and a Fraction of a Second Later

blocks.content: Before tracing the journey itself, it helps to name the destination this topic is walking toward: by the end, you should be able to describe, step by step, exactly what happens to your data between the click and the reply, without any of it feeling like magic.

Everything that follows builds on one central object: the packet. Once you understand what a packet is and how it moves, the rest of this chapter is really just following one packet, and its siblings, on their trip across the network.
2. Why Data Cannot Travel as One Giant Blob
blocks.text: 2. Why Data Cannot Travel as One Giant Blob

blocks.content: The obvious way to send a message would be to push it out as one continuous, unbroken stream of bits from start to finish. Real networks do not work that way, and the reason is simple: the links that make up a network are shared by everyone using them at the same time.

If one device sent one enormous unbroken stream, it would hog the line for as long as that stream lasted. Every other device waiting to use that same link, someone loading a webpage, someone on a video call, someone sending an email, would simply have to wait. Breaking data into smaller pieces solves this cleanly: many devices can share the same links fairly, taking turns, piece by piece, instead of one device monopolizing the whole connection.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867063-880384465.png
blocks.alt: Why Data Cannot Travel as One Giant Blob

blocks.title: One lane, many cars
blocks.content: Picture a single lane road. One very long truck moving end to end would block everyone behind it until it finally cleared the road. Now picture cars instead of a truck, each one short enough to interleave with other traffic. More cars move overall, and nobody waits nearly as long. Packets are the cars.

3. Packets: Small, Addressed, and Numbered

The pieces that data gets broken into are called packets. A packet is a small chunk of the original message, wrapped with just enough extra information to make sure it can find its way across the network and be understood correctly once it arrives.

Every packet carries three critical pieces of information alongside its actual data: a source address, saying where it came from; a destination address, saying where it is headed; and a sequence number, saying where this particular chunk fits within the original message. That sequence number is what makes reconstruction possible later, no matter what order the packets actually show up in.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867063-194811433.png

4. Different Packets, Different Paths

Here is an idea that surprises a lot of people the first time they hear it: packets belonging to the very same message do not all have to travel the same physical route across the network. One packet might cross through routers in one city, while the very next packet from the same message takes a completely different route, and both can still arrive correctly.

This works because each packet carries everything it needs entirely on its own terms. It carries its own complete addressing and sequence information, so it does not depend on traveling alongside the other packets from its message. Routers make an independent decision for every single packet that passes through them, based on current conditions, such as which paths are congested, which links are down, and which route looks fastest right now.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867064-621159710.png

blocks.title: Independent letters, same address
blocks.content: Imagine mailing four letters that together make up one long message, and each one gets carried by a different delivery route because that is whichever route happened to be fastest that day. As long as every letter has the full address and a page number written on it, it does not matter which road each one traveled. The recipient can still put them in order.
5. Hop by Hop: The Journey Through Routers
blocks.text: 5. Hop by Hop: The Journey Through Routers

blocks.content: A packet does not leap from source to destination in one single jump. It travels hop by hop, passing from router to router, with each router examining the destination address and forwarding the packet toward whichever neighboring router gets it closer to where it needs to go.

Think of it like a road trip where you stop and ask for directions at every landmark along the way. Nobody at the first stop knows the entire route to your final destination, but they know enough to point you toward the next landmark. Repeat that enough times, hop after hop, and you eventually arrive, even though no single point along the way ever held the full picture.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867064-965339822.png
blocks.alt: Hop by Hop: The Journey Through Routers

blocks.content: How a router actually decides which neighbor is the right next hop, using what is called a routing table, is worth a full topic on its own, and this course covers exactly that in the routing fundamentals topic later on. For now, the important picture to hold onto is this: the journey is made of many small hops, not one giant leap.

blocks.content: 6. Traceroute: Watching the Journey for Real
blocks.text: 6. Traceroute: Watching the Journey for Real

blocks.content: Everything described so far can sound abstract until you actually watch it happen. Traceroute is a real command line tool, available on basically every computer, that reveals the exact hop by hop path a packet takes to reach a destination, router by router, along with how long each hop took to respond.

Running it against any website shows you a numbered list of every router the packet passed through on the way there. It genuinely makes this whole chapter visible on a real, live network, and it is a tool worth trying yourself the moment you finish this topic, one that network engineers reach for constantly when something is slow and they need to find out exactly where the delay is happening.

7. Reassembly: Putting the Pieces Back Together
blocks.text: 7. Reassembly: Putting the Pieces Back Together

blocks.content: Every packet that makes it to the destination gets collected into a buffer, a temporary holding area, as it arrives. Because different packets can travel different routes and take different amounts of time, they frequently do not arrive in the same order they were sent.

This is exactly why the sequence number matters so much. The destination device looks at each arriving packet's sequence number and slots it into its correct position, regardless of the order it actually showed up in. Once every packet for the message has arrived and been placed correctly, the destination reconstructs the original, complete message and hands it up to whatever application is waiting for it, a browser, a chat app, a video call.

blocks.alt: Reassembly: Putting the Pieces Back Together

blocks.content: 8. When a Packet Does Not Arrive
blocks.text: 8. When a Packet Does Not Arrive

blocks.content: Not every packet sent actually makes it. Links get congested, routers get overloaded, cables get physically damaged, and wireless signals get interrupted. Packet loss is not some rare edge case, it is a normal, expected part of how real networks behave, and every reliable protocol is designed around the assumption that it will happen sometimes.

This topic will not go deep into how loss gets detected and fixed, that is a big enough subject to deserve its own full treatment. What matters here is the forward pointer: later in this course, the topic on TCP reliability covers exactly how a missing packet gets noticed, and how the sender figures out it needs to resend it, so that the destination still ends up with a complete, correct message even when something along the way went wrong.

blocks.title: A quick preview
blocks.content: The short version: the destination can tell a packet is missing because it sees a gap in the sequence numbers, seq 1, seq 2, seq 4 arrives with no seq 3 in sight. That gap is the trigger for a resend. The full mechanics of how and when that resend happens belong to the TCP reliability topic.
9. A Full Worked Example: One Message, Four Packets
blocks.text: 9. A Full Worked Example: One Message, Four Packets

blocks.content: Let's trace one specific message from start to finish, with concrete numbers attached, so the whole picture clicks into place at once. Say a device breaks a message into four packets, numbered 1 through 4, and sends them out across the network toward their destination.

Because of everything covered so far, those four packets do not have to travel together or arrive in order, and in this example they do not. Packet 3 happens to arrive first, then packet 1, then packet 4, then finally packet 2. To anyone watching the raw arrivals, that looks like chaos. To the destination device, it is not a problem at all.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867352-532973481.png
blocks.alt: A Full Worked Example: One Message, Four Packets

The destination never needed the packets to show up in order. It only needed every packet to eventually show up, and every packet to carry a sequence number telling it exactly where to slot in. The moment packet 2 finally arrives, the buffer has everything it needs, and the original message comes back together correctly, in the right order, exactly as it was written.
10. Why This Design Makes the Internet Resilient
blocks.text: 10. Why This Design Makes the Internet Resilient

blocks.content: This whole approach, breaking data into independent, addressed packets and letting each one find its own way, is not just a clever trick for sharing bandwidth. It is one of the biggest reasons the internet as a whole survives failures as well as it does.

Because packets are independent, a single router going down or a single link failing does not necessarily doom an entire message. The packets that already went a different way are unaffected, and the packets still in flight can often be rerouted around the failure entirely, through whichever routers and links are still working. No single point of the network has to stay healthy for the whole system to keep functioning.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436867352-769592704.png
blocks.alt: Why This Design Makes the Internet Resilient

blocks.title: Why this matters for engineers
blocks.content: This same idea, breaking work into independent pieces that do not all depend on one fragile path, shows up constantly in distributed systems design, well beyond networking. Understanding why packet switching survives failures is a genuinely useful mental model for building resilient systems of your own.
11. Common Mistakes

The single most common misunderstanding is picturing data traveling as one continuous stream, flowing smoothly from source to destination like water through a single hose for the entire distance. In reality, it is many small, independently addressed packets, each making its own way through the network, and often arriving out of order.

The second common mistake is assuming that all the packets belonging to one message must travel the identical path. They frequently do not. Routers make a fresh decision for every packet, and two packets from the same message can genuinely cross the network by completely different routes and still both arrive correctly, thanks to the addressing and sequence numbers each one carries.

["Wrong: data flows as one unbroken stream the whole way. Right: data is broken into many small, independently addressed packets.","Wrong: every packet from one message takes the same path. Right: routers decide the path for each packet independently, and paths can differ.","Wrong: packets that arrive out of order are an error. Right: out of order arrival is normal and expected, sequence numbers exist to fix it."]
